title: Quantum interpretation of classical LiF simulations
abstract: Recent studies have shown that classical LiF simulations can reproduce low-temperature experimental spectra when performed at a simulation temperature $T^*$ higher than the physical temperature $T$. We show that the characteristic scale of this rescaling follows naturally from quantum vibrational statistics. An effective temperature $T_{\rm eff}(T)$ is obtained by matching classical and quantum harmonic energies and is evaluated using an analytic acoustic-optical model and a first-principles LiF vibrational density of states $D(\varepsilon)$. The resulting temperature reproduces the low-temperature scale of the reported spectral temperature and approaches the physical temperature in the classical regime. Our results identify zero-point motion and Planck-Bose-Einstein statistics as the origin of the reported temperature scale.
summary: This work addresses the discrepancy between classical and quantum predictions for the vibrational spectra of LiF at low temperatures. By deriving an effective temperature ($T_{	ext{eff}}$) that bridges the gap, the authors show that the observed temperature rescaling is fundamentally rooted in zero-point motion and Planck-Bose-Einstein statistics. The results provide a quantum mechanical explanation for the temperature scale used in classical simulations.
main_problem: The paper investigates the origin of the temperature rescaling ($T^*$) observed when classical simulations of LiF infrared spectra reproduce low-temperature experimental data using a simulation temperature higher than the physical temperature.
main_result: The rescaling is attributed to quantum vibrational statistics, leading to an effective temperature ($T_{	ext{eff}}$) derived by matching quantum and classical vibrational energies.
method: The authors derive $T_{	ext{eff}}$ by equating the total vibrational energy calculated using quantum phonon statistics (Bose-Einstein distribution) to the classical energy, employing both an analytic model and a first-principles Density of States (DOS).
model_or_system: The system studied is the Lithium Fluoride (LiF) crystal. The model relies on the harmonic approximation and the vibrational density of states, $D(\epsilon)$, derived from first-principles calculations.
key_observables: Effective temperature ($T_{	ext{eff}}$), vibrational Helmholtz free energy ($F_{	ext{vib}}$), entropy ($S_{	ext{vib}}$), and heat capacity ($C_V$).
important_parameters: Physical temperature ($T$), simulation temperature ($T^*$), zero-point motion energy, and the characteristic temperature scale derived from the DOS.
main_assumptions: The harmonic approximation is used for calculating thermodynamic quantities, and the analysis compares quantum statistics (Planck-Bose-Einstein) against classical expectations.
figures_summary: The notes mention comparisons between quantum and classical predictions for thermodynamic functions, and specific numerical comparisons between calculated $T_{	ext{eff}}$ and reported spectral temperatures ($T^*$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by defining the effective temperature via energy matching, first using an analytic acoustic-optical model, and then refining the prediction using the full, first-principles calculated vibrational DOS.
why_interesting: The rigorous derivation of an effective temperature scale from fundamental quantum statistics (zero-point motion) to explain discrepancies in classical simulations is highly relevant to understanding quantum corrections in condensed matter systems.

The gray dashed line denotes the classical limit Teff = T. The inset enlarges the low-temperature region and shows the first-principles limiting value Teff(0) = 152.0 K.
FIG. 2: First-principles vibrational density of states of LiF per primitive cell. The two groups (acoustic and optical) are separated by a phonon gap.

FIG. 3: Quantum (solid lines) and classical canonical (dashed lines) harmonic thermodynamic functions of LiF obtained from the first-principles vibrational DOS normalized to six modes per primitive cell: (a) Helmholtz free energy, (b) entropy, and (c) constant-volume heat capacity. The zero-point contribution is included in the quantum free energy. The classical phase- space normalization is chosen so that the classical expressions reproduce the high-temperature limits of the quantum results. Classically, CV = 6R at all temperatures, whereas the entropy diverges to −∞as T →0; consequently, the vertical axis in panel (b) has been truncated.
